AbstractText.Label: OBJECTIVE
AbstractText.content: To investigate associations of various bio-psychosocial factors with bodily pain, physical func-tioning, and ability to work in low back pain.

AbstractText.Label: SUBJECTS
AbstractText.content: A total of 219 female healthcare workers with recurrent non-specific low back pain.

AbstractText.Label: METHODS
AbstractText.content: Associations between several physical and psychosocial factors and: (i) bodily pain, (ii) physical functioning and (iii) ability to work were studied. Variables with statistically significant associations (p < 0.05) in bivariate analysis were set within a generalized linear model to analyse their relationship with each dependent variable.

AbstractText.Label: RESULTS
AbstractText.content: In generalized linear model analysis, perceived work-induced lumbar exertion (p < 0.001), multi-site pain (p <0.001) and work-related fear-avoidance beliefs (FAB-W) (p = 0.02) best explained bodily pain. Multi-site pain (p < 0.001), lumbar exertion (p = 0.005), FAB-W (p = 0.01) and physical performance in figure-of-eight running (p = 0.01) and modified push-ups (p = 0.05) best explained physical functioning; FAB-W (p <0.001), lumbar exertion (p = 0.003), depression (p = 0.01) and recovery after work (p = 0.03) best explained work ability. In bivariate analysis lumbar exertion was associated with poor physical performance.

AbstractText.Label: CONCLUSION
AbstractText.content: FAB-W and work-induced lumbar exertion were associated with levels of pain, physical functioning and ability to work. Poor physical performance capacity was associated with work-induced lumbar exertion. Interventions that aim to reduce fear-avoidance and increase fitness capacity might be beneficial.
